title: Media Literacy - Navigating the Information Age
author: UI-TARS Team
description: How to spot fake news, understand bias, and be a smart consumer of information
learningObjectives: Understand what Media is (TV, Internet, Books)
Learn to distinguish Fact vs. Opinion
Explore the concept of 'Fake News' and misinformation

2-5.title: Real or Make-Believe?
2-5.description: Is that dragon real? Let's learn about stories and screens!

en.title: Real or Make-Believe?
en.welcome: Look at the TV! Look at the tablet! We see lots of pictures. But are they real?
en.mainContent:
**Real vs. Pretend:**
*   **Real:** A dog in the park. Your mommy. An apple you can eat.
*   **Pretend:** A dragon on TV. A cartoon mouse. A purple cow.
*   It's fun to pretend, but we know it's just a story!

**Commercials (Ads):**
*   Sometimes the TV shows us a cool toy. 'Buy this! It's the best!'
*   That is a **Commercial**. They want you to ask Mommy to buy it.
*   Is the toy really that cool? Maybe... or maybe they just made it look shiny.

**Scary Stuff:**
*   Sometimes we see scary things on the screen. Monsters! 
*   Remember: It's just a picture. It can't hurt you. You can turn it off! Click!

**Who made it?**
*   Someone drew the cartoon. Someone filmed the movie. 
*   Screens are like windows into other people's imaginations.
keyPoints: Some things are Real (Dog), some are Pretend (Dragon)
Commercials want you to buy things
You can turn off scary things
People make the things we see on screens
interactionPrompts: Is a unicorn Real or Pretend?
If a commercial says 'Best Toy Ever,' is it true?
Show me how you turn off the TV. Click!
en.wisdomMoment: You are the boss of your eyes. You choose what to watch.
en.cta: Draw a picture of something Real and something Pretend. Tell your parents which is which.
en.summary: You learned about Real vs. Pretend, Commercials, Scary Stuff, and Turning it Off!

es.title: ¿Real o Imaginario?

6-12.title: Media Detective: Finding the Truth
6-12.description: Fact vs. Opinion, Ads, and how to spot a lie

en.title: Media Detective: Finding the Truth
en.welcome: Put on your detective hat! Not everything you see on the internet is true. We need to investigate.
en.mainContent:
**Fact vs. Opinion:**
*   **Fact:** Something that can be proven true. 'The sky is blue.' 'Spiders have 8 legs.'
*   **Opinion:** What someone thinks or feels. 'Blue is the best color.' 'Spiders are scary.'
*   *Trick:* Sometimes people say opinions like they are facts! ('This is the best game ever!'). Be careful.

**Advertising (Ads):**
*   Ads are designed to make you want things. 
*   *Tricks:* Cool music, happy people, famous stars. 
*   *Targeting:* They know what you like (from your clicks) and show you ads for it. It's not magic; it's an algorithm.

**Fake News:** Stories that are made up to trick you. 
*   Why? To make money (clicks) or to make you angry.
*   *Clues:* Does it sound too crazy to be true? ('Aliens land in school!'). Check the source. Is it a real news site?

**Photoshopping:** Photos can be changed. People can make themselves look thinner, smoother, or add things that weren't there. Don't believe every picture.

**The 3 Questions:**
1.  Who made this?
2.  Why did they make it? (To sell? To inform? To entertain?).
3.  What is missing?
keyPoints: Fact (Provable) vs. Opinion (Feeling)
Ads use tricks to make you buy things
Fake News is made up to get clicks
Photos can be edited (Photoshop)
Ask: Who made this? Why?
interactionPrompts: Is 'Broccoli is yummy' a Fact or an Opinion?
Have you ever seen a photo that looked fake?
Why do YouTubers ask you to 'Like and Subscribe'? (Money!)
en.wisdomMoment: The truth is like a lion. You don't have to defend it. Let it loose. It will defend itself. (St. Augustine). But you have to find it first.
en.cta: Look at a cereal box. Read the words. Does it say 'Best Taste'? That's an opinion! Does it say '10g Sugar'? That's a fact!
en.summary: You've explored Fact vs. Opinion, Advertising Tricks, Fake News, Photoshop, and The 3 Questions.

Pourquoi les YouTubeurs demandent-ils de 'Liker et S'abonner'?

13-17.title: Media Literacy: Who Controls the Message?
13-17.description: Gatekeepers, algorithms, echo chambers, and propaganda

en.title: Media Literacy: Who Controls the Message?
en.welcome: Information is power. Whoever controls the information controls the world. In the past, it was Kings. Today, it is Tech Giants.
en.mainContent:
**Gatekeepers:** 
*   *Past:* Editors and Publishers decided what news you saw. They filtered out crazy stuff, but also suppressed minority voices.
*   *Present:* No Gatekeepers! Anyone can post anything. Freedom is high, but so is noise and lies.

**The Algorithm:** Social media sites (TikTok, Instagram) want you to stay on the app. 
*   They show you what makes you react (Anger, Fear, Laughter). 
*   They don't care if it's true; they care if it's *engaging*.

**Echo Chambers (Filter Bubbles):** The algorithm shows you opinions you already agree with. 
*   If you like cats, you see cats. 
*   If you hate a politician, you see posts hating that politician. 
*   You start to think *everyone* agrees with you. This creates polarization.

**Propaganda:** Information used to promote a political cause. 
*   *Techniques:* Name-calling, Bandwagon ('Everyone is doing it!'), Fear-mongering.
*   It's not just in history books; memes can be propaganda.

**Deepfakes:** AI can create videos of people saying things they never said. Seeing is no longer believing. We have to verify sources.

**Lateral Reading:** Don't just read the article. Open a new tab. Search for the author. Search for the claim. See what *other* sources say.
keyPoints: Gatekeepers are gone; Algorithms now curate our news
Algorithms prioritize engagement (Anger) over truth
Echo Chambers make us think everyone agrees with us
Propaganda uses emotion to manipulate
Deepfakes threaten reality
Lateral Reading is the best way to verify facts
interactionPrompts: Check your 'For You' page. What does the algorithm think you like?
Have you ever shared something without checking if it was true?
How can you tell if a video is a Deepfake?
en.wisdomMoment: If you don't pay for the product, you are the product. (Social Media adage). Your attention is being sold.
en.core_metaphor: The internet is a hall of mirrors
en.cta: Go to a news site you disagree with. Read one article. Try to understand their perspective. Break the Echo Chamber.
en.summary: You've explored Gatekeepers, Algorithms, Echo Chambers, Propaganda, Deepfakes, and Lateral Reading.

18-35.title: The Attention Economy: Reclaiming Your Mind
18-35.description: Dopamine loops, surveillance capitalism, and digital minimalism

en.title: The Attention Economy: Reclaiming Your Mind
en.welcome: Your attention is a finite resource. The smartest engineers in the world are paid millions to steal it from you. It's time to take it back.
en.mainContent:
**Surveillance Capitalism (Shoshana Zuboff):** Tech companies track your every move (location, clicks, pauses) to build a model of you. They sell predictions of your behavior to advertisers. 

**The Slot Machine in Your Pocket:** 
*   *Variable Reward:* You pull to refresh (pull the lever). Will you get a Like? A Message? Nothing? The uncertainty releases Dopamine. It is designed to be addictive.
*   *Infinite Scroll:* There is no stopping point. You can scroll forever. It removes the cue to stop.

**Impact on Cognition:** 
*   *Fragmented Attention:* We switch tasks every 40 seconds. We are losing the ability to 'Deep Work' (focus for hours).
*   *Memory:* We outsource memory to Google. We don't remember things; we remember where to find them.

**Digital Minimalism (Cal Newport):** 
*   Not anti-tech, but intentional tech. 
*   *Declutter:* Delete apps you don't love.
*   *Notifications:* Turn them OFF. You check the phone; don't let the phone check you.
*   *Solitude:* Spend time alone with your thoughts, without input. This is where creativity happens.

**The Right to Disconnect:** Some countries (France) have laws that bosses can't email you after work. We need mental rest.
keyPoints: Tech companies profit from your attention (Surveillance Capitalism)
Social media uses gambling psychology (Variable Reward) to addict you
Constant switching destroys focus and deep thinking
Digital Minimalism: Be intentional, not passive
Solitude is essential for a healthy mind
interactionPrompts: Check your 'Screen Time' stats. Are you shocked?
How do you feel when you leave your phone at home? (Anxious? Free?)
What could you do with the 2 hours a day you spend scrolling?
en.wisdomMoment: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives. (Annie Dillard). Don't scroll your life away.
en.cta: Turn off all non-human notifications (News, Games, Likes). Only keep texts/calls from real people. Try it for 24 hours.
en.summary: You've explored Surveillance Capitalism, Slot Machine Psychology, Fragmented Attention, Digital Minimalism, and Solitude.

36-60.title: Journalism: The Fourth Estate
36-60.description: The role of the press in democracy, objectivity vs. fairness, and citizen journalism

en.title: Journalism: The Fourth Estate
en.welcome: Thomas Jefferson said he would rather have newspapers without a government than a government without newspapers. A free press is the immune system of democracy.
en.mainContent:
**The Fourth Estate:** The press acts as a check on the three branches of government (Executive, Legislative, Judicial). It holds power accountable. 'Comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable.'

**Objectivity vs. Fairness:** 
*   *Objectivity:* Trying to be neutral. (Hard, because humans are biased).
*   *Fairness:* Giving everyone a chance to speak, but not creating 'False Equivalence.' (If one person says it's raining and another says it's dry, the journalist's job is to look out the window, not just quote both).

**Investigative Journalism:** Deep digging. Watergate (Woodward and Bernstein) brought down a President. Spotlight (Boston Globe) exposed abuse in the church. It takes time and money.

**The Crisis of Local News:** Local newspapers are dying (craigslist killed classified ads; Facebook took ad revenue). 
*   *Result:* Corruption increases in local government because no one is watching. 'News Deserts.'

**Citizen Journalism:** Everyone with a phone is a reporter. 
*   *Pros:* Immediate, raw, covers things mainstream media misses (George Floyd video).
*   *Cons:* No verification, no ethics code, can spread rumors fast.

**Supporting the Truth:** Good journalism costs money. If we want truth, we have to pay for subscriptions.
keyPoints: A free press is essential for democracy (The Fourth Estate)
Journalists should seek Truth, not just 'balance' (False Equivalence)
Investigative Journalism exposes corruption
The death of local news hurts communities
Citizen Journalism is powerful but risky
We must support journalism financially
interactionPrompts: Do you pay for any news? Why or why not?
Can a journalist ever be truly neutral?
What happens to a town when the newspaper closes?
en.wisdomMoment: Democracy dies in darkness. (Washington Post slogan). Light is the best disinfectant.
en.cta: Read a local news story about your town. What is the city council doing? Be informed.
en.summary: You've explored The Fourth Estate, Objectivity, Investigative Journalism, Local News Crisis, and Citizen Journalism.

61-102.title: The Wisdom of Silence: Unplugging
61-102.description: Information overload, the value of silence, and deep reading

en.title: The Wisdom of Silence: Unplugging
en.welcome: We live in an age of noise. Information Overload (Infobesity) is stressing our brains. Silence is no longer empty; it is a luxury product.
en.mainContent:
**Information Overload:** We consume 34 gigabytes of information a day. Our brains were not designed for this. It leads to 'Continuous Partial Attention' and burnout.

**Deep Reading vs. Skimming:** 
*   *Skimming (F-Pattern):* How we read online. Scanning for keywords. Fast, shallow.
*   *Deep Reading:* How we read a book. Slow, immersive, linear. This builds empathy and critical thinking. We are losing this skill (The Shallows).

**The Value of Boredom:** When you are bored, your brain goes into 'Default Mode Network.' This is where daydreaming, problem-solving, and creativity happen. If you fill every gap with a phone, you kill creativity.

**Digital Sabbath:** Taking one day a week off screens. (e.g., Sundown Friday to Sundown Saturday). 
*   *Benefits:* Better sleep, deeper conversations, time for hobbies, feeling 'time affluence.'

**Elders as Anchors:** You remember a world before the internet. You know how to wait, how to be alone, how to fix things. Teach the young the value of the analog world.
keyPoints: Information Overload causes stress and burnout
Deep Reading builds brain power; Skimming erodes it
Boredom is the birthplace of creativity
Digital Sabbath restores balance
Elders hold the wisdom of the analog world
interactionPrompts: Do you feel like you have 'too much' information?
When was the last time you read a book for 2 hours without stopping?
Could you do a 'Digital Sabbath'?
en.wisdomMoment: Silence is a source of great strength. (Lao Tzu). In the silence, you find yourself.
en.cta: Leave your phone in another room for 1 hour. Read a book or look out the window. Resist the urge to check.
en.summary: You've explored Information Overload, Deep Reading, Boredom, Digital Sabbath, and Analog Wisdom.
